title: Walking cramp, kick cramp and Duke Ellington's Main Stem
summary: Green restates the cramps, describes his walks around Harlem and Seventh Avenue as the main stem, and hearing Ellington's Main Stem at Bubbles' house.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Mr. Nierenberg: This is tape number nine.

Now, as I was saying, we were speaking about the walking cramp and the kick cramp, and the difference in the qualities. (Unintelligible) the kick cramp was much richer than the walking cramp, which is absolutely true. Because that is so. The walking cramp is on one foot, and the kicking cramp is two, on two feet. And that's what happened. So I was in the midst of it all, and I was trying to teach myself different ways of doing a tap step more than one way. So I had a little tour that I used to go on and I wandered as far down as what they called the Hoofer's Club. That was down there by the Lafayette Theater, at 131st and 7th Avenue. Now, 7th Avenue was known as the main stem at that time, and eventually Duke Ellington composed a song, a jazz song, called "Main Stem". I think I have the record. And Mr. Bubbles was saying that that was one of his favorite pieces of music. So one time we had the radio on, in Mr. Bubbles' house, and this piece came over the radio, "Main Stem", and the Duke Ellington Orchestra, you see. And it was gorgeous jazz music, you know, this "Main Stem", and if anyone ever achieved a tap dance to this,
I think they would reach the heights of stardom, because it's really brilliant.
